tip: French splits 'know' in two: connaître for people and places you're familiar with, savoir for facts. A doctor is someone you know, so 'je connais un bon médecin'.
'Est-ce que' literally means 'is it that' – drop it in front of a statement and it turns into a yes/no question with no word-order change: 'Est-ce que tu connais...'.
English drops the article in 'any questions', but French keeps it: 'des questions'. Des is the plural of un/une and can't be skipped.
'Personne' means nobody, but it still needs 'ne' before the verb – and no 'pas': 'personne ne connaissait' = nobody knew.
'Le dimanche' with the article means 'on Sundays' as a habit, not one specific Sunday. Drop the 'le' and it's just this coming Sunday.
France runs on a 24-hour clock: 'dix-huit heures' (eighteen hours) is 6 PM. Add 12 to any afternoon time to get the everyday form.
Start a sentence with 'peut-être' and the verb jumps ahead of the subject: 'devrions-nous'. To skip the inversion, say 'peut-être qu'on...' instead.
French weather runs on 'faire': 'il faisait froid' is literally 'it was making cold'. Heat works the same way – 'il fait chaud'.
'S'attendre à' means to expect, not to wait – and it's reflexive with 'à': 'je ne m'attendais pas à ce résultat' = I didn't expect this.
'On' is the everyday stand-in for 'you/one/people in general': 'on entendait' = you could hear. It always takes the il/elle verb form.
'Chercher' already includes 'for': 'je cherchais un restaurant' = I was looking for a restaurant. Never add 'pour' after it.
To love something in general, French adds 'les': 'adorions les vacances' = loved vacations. English drops the article here; French never does.
With 'depuis', French stays in the present for something still true: 'nous le connaissons depuis l'enfance' = we've known him since childhood.
'Jouer à' is for games and sports: 'jouaient aux cartes' = played cards (à + les = aux). Instruments switch to 'jouer de'.
'Se souvenir' needs both a reflexive pronoun and 'de': 'te souvenais de cette chanson' = remembered this song. The 'de' is not optional.
'Quatre à quatre' literally means 'four by four' – the image is taking the stairs four steps at a time, i.e. bounding down them fast.
